summary: Worse than the pre-2025 position, and worse than Wales on official posture. The EHRC's updated Code of Practice for Services, Public Functions and Associations was laid 21 May 2026 and came into force on 5 August 2026 as statutory guidance (replacing the 2011 code): single-sex spaces open to the public — toilets, gym changing rooms, hospital wards, rape-crisis centres — should be organised by biological sex, with trans people directed to gender-neutral or birth-sex facilities. The guidance binds service providers UK-wide but is administered in England, and it is the map's clearest 'you may be refused' signal. Its legal predicate is For Women Scotland v The Scottish Ministers (UK Supreme Court, 16 April 2025): 'sex' and 'woman' in the Equality Act 2010 mean biological/registered sex, and a Gender Recognition Certificate does not change legal sex for Equality Act purposes. The ruling has immediate visitor-facing consequences in England's transport and custody settings: following it, British Transport Police moved (17 April 2025, stated interim position) to strip-searching trans women detained on the rail network by male officers, reversing the acquired-gender policy for GRC holders. Anti-trans offending is statistically invisible in the official record: England and Wales reported 115,990 hate crimes in the year to March 2025 across five monitored strands, and transgender identity is not a separately recorded strand (unlike Scotland and Northern Ireland). The strongest practical gradient inside the unit is London — visible community, dedicated services, dedicated hate-crime policing — versus the rest of England; no sourced sub-England region-level evidence was found, so the unit is assessed whole.

sources.summary: BBC News (19 June 2026): a judge (Lady Ross, Court of Session) ruled Scottish Prison Service guidance allowing some trans prisoners to be housed by gender identity unlawful — sex segregation in prisons must be based on biological sex, applying the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 'definition of a woman' ruling. The judgment confirms the biological-sex custody logic that the same UK-wide ruling imposes on England's prison and custody decisions; the first minister said the government will consider the judgment (the Supreme Court had already held Article 8 confers no automatic right to opposite-biological-sex accommodation).

BBC News (5 February 2026): argument of the same judicial review, in which government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy 'Orwellian'; the case tests how far the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 ruling (cited as the predicate for England's EHRC code and BTP strip-search policy) reaches into prison accommodation UK-wide.

The Guardian (17 April 2025): British Transport Police amended its custody strip-searching policy after the UK Supreme Court gender ruling — same-sex searches in custody now to be 'undertaken in accordance with the biological birth sex of the detainee', meaning trans women arrested on Britain's railways (whose network is overwhelmingly in England) are strip-searched by male officers; the previous policy searched GRC holders by acquired gender. BTP called it an 'interim position while we digest yesterday's judgment' — a direct, visitor-facing practice change.
